title: LCA of an Aluminium Beverage Can: The Power of Recycled Content
sub: A cradle-to-grave assessment of a 330 ml aluminium can comparing 100% virgin, 70% recycled and 100% recycled aluminium, and a low-carbon primary metal pathway.
pdf: Case 04 — LCA of an Aluminium Beverage Can: Executive Summary
fu: Packaging of 330 ml of a carbonated soft drink in one aluminium can, delivered and consumed in Germany
ref: One 13 g can (body and end), including 0.2 g coatings, filled, distributed and collected
boundary: Cradle-to-grave: bauxite mining, alumina refining, smelting, casting and rolling, can making and coating, filling, distribution and chilling, collection, remelting and secondary aluminium production
geo: Primary aluminium at global-average production mix; can making, filling and use in Germany
method: EF 3.1 characterisation; IPCC AR6 GWP100; AWARE for water scarcity
alloc: Cut-off (recycled-content) approach as the main method; the avoided-burden (end-of-life recycling) approach is discussed in interpretation because it changes results for highly recyclable metals
cutoff: Flows <1% of mass and energy excluded (lubricants, inks) with cumulative exclusions <5%
dq: International Aluminium Institute and European Aluminium data; ecoinvent; industry can-weight benchmarks. Overall data quality Medium–High; Medium for primary origin
srcShort: Illustrative model; parameters within ranges from the International Aluminium Institute, European Aluminium, Metal Packaging Europe and ecoinvent.
loop: Circular loop: can-to-can recycling; remelting uses about 5% of the energy of primary production
exec:
This case study assesses a 330 ml aluminium beverage can and how its footprint changes with recycled content. Aluminium is a strategic material: primary production is among the most electricity-intensive industrial processes, yet the metal can be recycled repeatedly without loss of quality, and beverage cans are one of the best-collected packaging types in Europe.
With 100% virgin aluminium from the global-average production mix, the illustrative result is 0.246 kg CO2e per can. Smelting alone contributes 66%, driven by coal-based electricity in major producing regions and by process emissions from anodes. Can making, filling, distribution and chilling together add about 0.04 kg.
Using 70% recycled aluminium cuts the result by about 54% to 0.114 kg CO2e; 100% recycled content cuts it by about 77% to 0.057 kg. A pathway combining 70% recycled content with hydro-powered primary metal and a renewable-powered can plant reaches 0.062 kg CO2e.
The main recommendation is to maximise recycled content and secure low-carbon primary metal, while supporting high collection rates so that scrap is available. Recycled content is limited by scrap supply, so claims must reflect system-wide availability. For CSRD, results support ESRS E1 (Scope 3 Category 1 and transition plan), E5 (recycled content and recyclability) and E2 (bauxite residue and smelter emissions).
overview:
The aluminium beverage can is made from rolled sheet that is cupped, drawn, ironed, coated, printed and necked at high speed. The can body and end together weigh about 13 g. Most of the environmental burden is embedded in the metal before it reaches the can maker.
The purpose of this LCA is to show how metal sourcing (virgin vs recycled, and the energy source of primary smelting) changes the footprint, and how these results inform procurement and climate targets.
goal: The goal is to support a beverage brand's packaging procurement and Scope 3 decarbonisation by quantifying the impact of aluminium sourcing choices. The audience is procurement, packaging and climate-strategy teams. Results are for internal decision-making.

stages.what: Bauxite is mined, then refined into alumina using the Bayer process (caustic soda, heat).
stages.in: Bauxite, caustic soda, heat (natural gas, coal), water
stages.ew: ≈0.45 MJ and 0.35 L water per can
stages.wa: Bauxite residue ≈33 g per can, stored in impoundments
stages.tr: Bauxite shipped from Guinea or Australia
stages.so: Land rights and community impacts around mines

stages.what: Alumina is electrolysed into aluminium in Hall-Héroult cells.
stages.em: CO2 from electricity and anodes; perfluorocarbons
stages.tr: Ingot to rolling mill, sea and rail
stages.as: Global average grid intensity for smelting ≈0.8 kg CO2e/kWh

stages.what: Ingots and recycled scrap are melted, cast and hot/cold rolled into can-body sheet.
stages.in: Primary ingot, scrap, natural gas, electricity

stages.what: Sheet is cupped, drawn and ironed, washed, coated, printed and necked; ends are made separately.
stages.em: CO2; volatile organic compounds from coatings
stages.wa: Process scrap (recycled in a closed loop)

stages.what: Cans are filled, seamed and pasteurised or cooled.
Transport to retail and refrigerated display.
Used cans are collected (deposit-return or kerbside), sorted with eddy-current separators and remelted.
stages.tr: Collection and transport to remelter, 400 km
stages.as: 75% collected for recycling (EU-level order of magnitude); remelting allocated to the next product (cut-off)

lci: Grid carbon intensity (global average for smelting)
300 km × 0.36 kg filled can incl. packaging

hot.why: Smelting uses about 14 kWh per kg of aluminium. On coal-based grids this makes it the dominant climate and energy hotspot (≈66%).
Carbon anodes are consumed and release CO2, and anode effects release perfluorocarbons with very high GWP.
About 2.5 kg of alkaline bauxite residue is generated per kg of aluminium, creating long-term storage and pollution risks; mining affects land and communities.
Low collection or exports of scrap force more primary metal into the system; recycled content is only as good as the collection system that feeds it.

desc: Global-average primary metal; renewable share low
Closed-loop can-to-can recycling only (not scalable for the whole market)
70% recycled; remaining primary from hydro-powered smelters; renewable electricity and heat at the can plant

sens.t: Sensitivity: carbon intensity of smelter electricity
sens.xl: Carbon intensity of smelting electricity (kg CO₂e/kWh)
sens.note: The energy source of primary smelting is the most influential parameter for virgin metal; recycled content reduces sensitivity to it.
sens.interp: A hydro-powered virgin can (0.107 kg) is below a coal-powered 70% recycled can only at the extremes. Both levers matter, and the origin of primary metal must be known to report credible numbers.

ci.stage: Primary smelting dominates the virgin can; everything after the rolling mill contributes less than 20%.
ci.stage_e: Smelting electricity accounts for about 60% of cumulative energy demand.
ci.stage_w: Water is used mainly in alumina refining and filling; overall volumes are small.
ci.donut: Two-thirds of the climate result occurs in one process step, so a single procurement choice (metal origin and recycled content) has outsized influence.
ci.sankey: Producing 13 g of aluminium needs about 58 g of bauxite and leaves 33 g of bauxite residue. Each can that is collected returns about 9.4 g of secondary aluminium.
ci.heat: Smelting is the hotspot for climate and energy; bauxite and alumina for land, water and toxicity.
ci.scen: Recycled content cuts the footprint most; low-carbon primary metal removes most of what remains.
ci.radar: Recycled scenarios reduce every indicator, especially waste (bauxite residue) and energy.
ci.wf: Recycled content and primary metal origin together deliver more than 95% of the reduction.

interp.m: The can's footprint is essentially the footprint of its metal. Recycled aluminium and low-carbon primary aluminium reduce it by up to about three quarters.
interp.a: Recycled content; smelter electricity source; recycling allocation method; collection rate.
interp.u: Primary metal origin is often unknown to buyers; scrap availability limits recycled content; allocation choices (cut-off vs avoided burden) can change rankings against other materials.
interp.can: Recycled content and smelter energy source are the dominant levers; downstream operations are minor.
interp.cannot: The study cannot show that every can could be 100% recycled (global scrap supply is insufficient), nor that aluminium is better than other materials in general.
interp.d: Metal procurement specifications, supplier decarbonisation requirements, support for collection systems, and Scope 3 target setting for packaging.

recs: Keep cans mono-material and unpigmented where possible; continue lightweighting ends and bodies.
Specify recycled content and low-carbon primary aluminium with verified product carbon footprints and chain-of-custody (e.g., ASI certification).
Electrify or decarbonise furnaces; maximise closed-loop process scrap; use renewable electricity at can plants.
Support deposit-return systems and avoid mixing cans with non-recyclable packaging formats.
Maximise collection and keep used cans within can-to-can loops rather than downcycling.
Report recycled content with chain-of-custody evidence; distinguish pre- and post-consumer scrap; avoid double counting of recycling benefits.
Support deposit-return systems and low-carbon primary production; address scrap export leakage.

take: An aluminium can's footprint is set by its metal: recycled content and low-carbon smelting can cut it by around three quarters, provided collection systems keep scrap in the loop.
biz: Contract for high recycled content and verified low-carbon primary aluminium, support deposit-return collection to secure scrap, and report recycled content with chain-of-custody evidence.
assume: Global-average primary aluminium (≈15 kg CO2e/kg); 13 g can; 75% collection; remelting 0.6 kg CO2e/kg; cut-off allocation. 100% recycled content is a closed-loop thought experiment, not a market-wide option.
